Introduction:
Gastric cancer (GC) remains one of the most common cancers worldwide [ 1 ]. Evidence increasingly indicates the effectiveness of endoscopic screening in reducing GC mortality [ 2–4 ]. Since 2002, South Korea has implemented nationwide GC screening for individuals aged 40 and older, and both individual-level and population-level studies have indicated that this program reduced GC mortality [ 3 , 5 ]. As encouraging evidence accumulates, an increasing number of countries are considering implementing organized GC screening programs to reduce GC burden [ 4 , 6 , 7 ]. Yet, one critical aspect of GC screening’s effect remains unresolved.

In addition to lowering mortality, GC screening is anticipated to prevent new cases by detecting and treating precancerous lesions [ 8 ]. However, the effect on GC incidence remains unclear, with conflicting findings from a limited number of individual-level studies [ 8–10 ]. South Korea’s pioneering screening program offers an opportunity for population-level analysis. Data from South Korea show that the age-standardized incidence of GC initially remained stable and later slightly declined during the screening period [ 11 ]. But disentangling the true effect of the screening program from other confounding factors and secular trends, especially given that national cancer data only began in 1999 [ 12 ], presents a significant challenge.

This study bypasses that limitation by using a quasi-experimental design and nearly three decades of high-quality data from the Seoul Cancer Registry (established in the early 1990s) to evaluate the impact of the screening program on GC incidence. By analyzing real-world data in complex settings, this study provides actionable insights for policymakers.
Methods:
### Research setting

In 1999, the Korean government launched a screening program for GC targeting low-income Medical Aid recipients. In 2002, the Korean National Cancer Screening Program (KNCSP) was expanded nationwide to include the National Health Insurance beneficiaries, resulting in almost universal coverage for all Korean citizens [ 5 ]. The KNCSP offers biennial screening for individuals aged 40 years and older, with a choice of upper gastrointestinal (UGI) series or endoscopy [ 13 ]. Two key trends have occurred since its implementation. First, national surveys indicate that the screening participation rate rose from 39.2% in 2004 to 77.5% in 2023 [ 14 ]. Second, the screening modality used has shifted dramatically. Among all screenings performed, the proportions conducted by endoscopy increased from 31.15% in 2002 to 72.55% in 2011 [ 13 ]. By 2019, nearly 90% of GC screenings were performed using endoscopy [ 15 ]. Details on the GC screening program are described in the Supplementary Methods .

### Study design

We used the synthetic control method (SCM) [ 16 ] to construct a synthetic control for Seoul by deriving a weighted average of multiple control registries without intervention. Weights were determined through a data-driven approach that minimized differences in age-standardized GC incidence between Seoul and the synthetic control prior to screening implementation. The SCM assumes that if the treated registry and constructed control registry have similar long-term GC incidence trajectories, they are likely influenced by similar driving factors and should continue to follow similar trends unless disrupted by an intervention, such as the start of screening in Seoul. Thus, any observed differences after the implementation start can be reasonably ascribed to the intervention.

This study was exempt from ethical review because it only used aggregated data.

### Outcome data

The primary outcome measure was age-standardized GC (International Classification of Diseases code: C16.0-C16.9) incidence among people aged 40 years or above. We obtained annual age-specific GC incidence rates for Seoul from the Seoul Cancer Registry (1993–2020), which covers 18% of South Korea’s total population. Control registry data were extracted from the Cancer Incidence in Five Continents (CI5) Plus database [ 17 ]. The CI5 plus database provides updated annual incidence rates from high-quality cancer registries. The primary quality indicators CI5 uses are the percentage of microscopic verification (MV%) and the percentage of cases registered by death certificate only (DCO%), where higher MV% and lower DCO% indicate better quality. The data were last updated in November 2024 and include records up to 2017. Age-standardized rates were calculated using the World Health Organization standard population age structure [ 18 ]. The main SCM analysis covered 1993–2017, while alternative analyses with only Seoul’s data extended to 2020, depending on data availability.

### Control registry selection

Control registries without organized GC screening programs were included in the donor pool based on the following criteria: (i) having GC incidence data for each year during the study period; (ii) being a single, primary registry. To prevent double-counting, we excluded combined registries [like “Thailand (four registries)”] or sub-registries (like “USA, California, Los Angeles: White”) when their individual or parent-level registries were available; (iii) reporting over 100 GC cases in 1993; (iv) having complete report of age-group specific population numbers. Supplementary Fig. S1 shows the selection procedure for the donor pools. Following these criteria, 30 registries met these criteria, and final control weights were assigned using data-driven processes as described in the statistical analysis section.

### Statistical analysis

The original SCM proposed by Abadie and Gardeazabal [ 19 ] in 2003 is designed to interpolate the outcomes of control units to prevent irrational counterfactuals. A requirement of this approach is the “convex hull” criterion, meaning the outcome of the treated units must remain inside the distribution of the control data. South Korea, however, has one of the highest rates of GC incidence in the world [ 20 ], which is insufficient to fulfill the convex hull condition [ 21 ]. Therefore, we applied the flexible SCM approach developed by Bonander [ 16 ], which relaxes the requirement for control weights to sum to one while imposing a penalty on extrapolation to avoid unrealistic estimates. Details on the construction of the synthetic control are in the Supplementary Methods .

We assessed pre-treatment fit by plotting the difference in GC incidence between Seoul and the synthetic control for all pre-treatment years. We calculated average post-intervention rate ratios (RRs) and their associated 95% confidence intervals (CIs). The average RR during the post-intervention period was estimated by dividing the treated unit’s average outcome values by the synthetic control’s average GC incidence for the same period. A three-fold cross-fitting method was applied to produce the final debiased estimate and its 95% CIs [ 16 ]. We also calculated the rate difference and RRs in each year during the post-intervention period. To assess whether the observed effects for Seoul could occur by chance, a placebo test was conducted by repeating the SCM for each control registry as if it were the intervention unit [ 3 ]. We then plotted the differences between observed and counterfactual trends for each control registry and Seoul to observe whether the effect for Seoul became distinct after the screening, suggesting it was unlikely due to randomness.

Several sensitivity analyses were conducted to evaluate the robustness of our findings. First, we performed the negative control outcome analysis by repeating the SCM among people aged 35–39, who did not undergo screening. If a difference in post-intervention trend is also observed for this population ineligible for screening, the observed effect in the main analyses may be due to other factors than screening. Second, we conducted the leave-one-out examination for each weighted control unit to test the influence of each single control registry’s weight. Third, the pre-intervention period was refined from 1993–2001 to 1993–98 to mitigate overfitting risks. The fit between Seoul and the synthetic control during the validation period (1999–2001) was assessed. A good fit during this period would confirm the SCM’s predictive validity for Seoul in the absence of the GC screening program.

We also employed various alternative methods. First, we borrowed the idea of the difference-in-differences (DID) analysis to account for background secular trends in incidence. This analysis compared the change in log age-standardized GC incidence between the pre- and post-intervention periods for the screening target population against the corresponding change observed in a non-eligible control population (aged 20–39). The resulting estimate (β), which is on the log scale, was converted to a relative percentage change for interpretation using the standard transformation ( e β - 1 ) * 100 % ⁠ . Second, following the method by Gangnon et al. [ 22 ] we conducted a modified age-period-cohort (APC) analysis [ 22 ] to evaluate screening’s impact on GC incidence by including a screening period function. The population and GC case data from the Seoul Cancer Registry were used to fit the negative binomial log-linear regression. The screening function allowed us to estimate the effect of screening on GC incidence. We also estimated the GC incidence without screening, which was derived as the sum of the age, period, and cohort effects. Details on the two alternative methods are in the Supplementary Methods . Data analyses were performed using R version 4.3.2.
Results:
The synthetic control was made up of 19 control registries, with Belarus emerging as the primary contributor ( Supplementary Table S1 ). The pre-intervention fit between Seoul and the synthetic control was good, showing similar decreasing trends in both ( Fig. 1 ). Following the initiation of the screening program, GC incidence in Seoul remained relatively stable compared to the decreasing trend in the synthetic control, showing a relatively higher rate with an average post-intervention RR being 1.11 (95% CI: 0.99–1.24). Notably, the magnitude of this difference was not static; it peaked in 2011 (at a relative 26%) and subsequently decreased ( Fig. 1 , Supplementary Table S2 ). During the pre-intervention period, the disparities between the synthetic control and Seoul were relatively minor compared to post-implementation differences ( Fig. 1A ). The post-intervention differences between the synthetic control and Seoul became markedly pronounced after 2005, as evident from the placebo tests ( Fig. 1B ).

Sensitivity analyses consistently demonstrated the robustness of our findings. Negative control outcome analysis showed no post-intervention differences in GC incidence in 35–39-year-olds who did not undergo screening ( Supplementary Fig. S2 ). This suggests that factors other than GC screening remained relatively stable and did not alter GC incidence. Excluding each weighted control registry had minimal impact on the base case analyses, and also when excluding the primary contributor, Belarus ( Supplementary Fig. S3 ). To validate the SCM’s ability to model Seoul’s underlying GC trend, we conducted a sensitivity analysis by restricting the pre-intervention period to 1993–1998. The resulting synthetic control accurately tracked Seoul’s actual declining incidence during this 1999–2001 validation period ( Supplementary Fig. S4 ). Furthermore, post-intervention differences between 2002 and 2017 resembled the main results, further corroborating the validity of our findings.

The naive DID analysis compared the change in GC incidence from the pre- to post-intervention period between the screening population and the population aged 20–39 years. This analysis showed that the implementation of screening was associated with a 9.4% relative increase in GC incidence in the screening group, after accounting for the underlying trend observed in the population aged 20–39 years ( Supplementary Fig. S5 ). Additionally, the effect trend indicated by the modified APC analysis aligned with the SCM results. The effect expanded over time, peaking at an RR of 1.14 (95% CI 1.03–1.28) between 2008 and 2012, but subsequently declined, showing a negative effect of 0.89 (95% CI 0.71–1.11) between 2018 and 2020 ( Fig. 2A ). Correspondingly, the observed GC incidence after screening was initially relatively higher but decreased from 2018 to 2020 compared to the estimated rate without screening ( Fig. 2B ).
Discussion:
Using population-based cancer registry data and a quasi-experimental design, our SCM analysis found that Seoul’s screening program initially increased GC incidence compared to the synthetic control, peaking at a 26% difference in the tenth year. In the final years of the SCM analysis, this gap began to narrow. These findings were consistent across sensitivity analyses. The trend was also consistent with our alternative APC model, which used an extended dataset for Seoul. The APC analysis suggested the narrowing trend continued and reversed into a reduction by the fifteenth year.

Researchers have long focused on the impact of GC screening on GC mortality [ 2–4 ], leading to a growing consensus regarding its beneficial effect in reducing mortality rates [ 6 , 7 ]. However, the effect of screening on GC incidence has received limited attention [ 9 ], despite its importance in providing a complete picture of the benefits and potential harms associated with screening programs. Insights from other cancer screenings, which have been more thoroughly investigated, underscores the importance of examining incidence separately, even when the benefit on mortality is well-established. For instance, colorectal cancer (CRC) screening has demonstrated a reduction effect on cancer incidence by the removal of precancerous lesions [ 23 ]. Conversely, breast cancer screening has been associated with increased cancer incidence due to overdiagnosis, which can lead to unnecessary medical interventions and psychological stress for patients. It should be noted that overdiagnosis still exists in CRC screening, despite its proven net reduction in CRC incidence [ 24 ]. These findings suggest that the impact of cancer screening on incidence is complex and can be distinct from its effect on mortality.

Published individual-level analyses regarding the effect of endoscopic screening on GC incidence showed mixed results [ 8–10 ]. A meta-analysis that included only four studies did not find the association between endoscopic screening and GC incidence [ 9 ]. However, two cohort studies conducted in high-GC-incidence regions of China observed that endoscopic screening reduced non-cardia GC incidence, but not cardia GC incidence, in the screened group compared to the unscreened group, after adjusting for age and sex [ 8 , 10 ].

Several factors may contribute to uncertainty and pose research challenges. First, screening initially inflates incidence rates by detecting prevalent disease, requiring a long-term follow-up to ascertain the ultimate effect. Second, endoscopic screening may allow for endoscopic resection of visible dysplasia, potentially reducing GC incidence. Endoscopic screening can also facilitate the detection and treatment of Helicobacter pylori infection, thereby preventing GC incidence. However, unlike CRC screening, where even low-risk polyps can be removed during colonoscopy, few treatments are available for atrophic gastritis and intestinal metaplasia during GC screening. Subsequent surveillance and treatment may be necessary, and even after curative removal of gastric dysplasia, there is a risk of metachronous gastric carcinoma.

The impact of a screening program on GC incidence, as assessed in this study, shows an even more complex dynamic when examining cross-sectional rates from a population perspective compared to cumulative incidence rates from a single cohort perspective. An initial rise in incidence is expected due to detecting asymptomatic GCs. The growing participation rates in the Korean GC screening program may further amplify and prolong this relative increase [ 14 ]. Additionally, the proportion of screenings conducted by endoscopy, known for its higher sensitivity compared to UGI series, has steadily increased [ 13 , 25 ]. Supporting these trends, the percentage of early-stage GC grew from 39% in 2001 to 73% in 2016 [ 26 ], suggesting that the increase in incidence is primarily attributable to early-stage GC detection. However, the potential for overdiagnosis in GC screening also warrants consideration [ 27 ]. Overdiagnosis in GC screening has rarely been investigated [ 27 ] and cannot be excluded as a possibility.

We also observed a diminishing relative increase of GC incidence after 2011, followed by a subsequent reduction effect. This pattern may suggest a compensatory drop following early detection or a potential preventive effect of screening. Given that our population is dynamic rather than fixed, and our outcome measures annual population incidence rates rather than cumulative incidence, we cannot discern these potential screening effects on GC incidence, as well as inferring which one dominates. The ultimate impact of screening on GC incidence remains uncertain, and randomized controlled trials are needed for conclusive determination.

A key strength of this study is its population-level evaluation of GC screening, which facilitates evidence triangulation. We confirmed the robustness of our primary SCM by extensively validating its predictive fit against observed GC trends using both a hold-out validation period ( Supplementary Fig. S4 ) and a negative control population ( Supplementary Fig. S2 ). We further employed methodological triangulation with APC and DID analyses. While these alternative models have more significant limitations than SCM in our case, particularly the naive DID, they corroborated the SCM’s findings and allowed us to analyze recent data from 2018 to 2020 that the SCM could not.

Our study has several limitations. First, the basic idea behind SCM is that once the synthetic control reproduces the treated unit’s pre-intervention outcome trajectory, it implicitly adjusts for all observed and unobserved factors influencing the outcome. As a result, adding explicit covariates is optional, because the synthetic control is already, by construction, comparable to the treated unit. Still, incorporating covariates can further strengthen the analysis [ 28 ]. In our study, we did not include covariates such as Helicobacter pylori infection rate due to limited data availability. Second, the increase in opportunistic GC screening in South Korea over time [ 29 ] might lead to an overestimated direct effect of the organized screening program on GC incidence. However, the start of the organized screening program might have had an indirect effect of improving coverage and quality of opportunistic screening. Third, we cannot discern the specific contributions of screening by UGI series or endoscopy to the observed effects. While UGI series was the main modality in the program’s early years, it was soon replaced by the more sensitive endoscopy.

As more countries consider organized GC screening or surveillance [ 4 , 6 , 7 ], South Korea’s GC screening program offers practical insights, but its generalizability requires caution. Endoscopy capacity is central to the screening and diagnosis of GC. In South Korea, the number of endoscopic examinations for GC increased 20-fold in the decade following the program’s start [ 30 ]. Such an increase will lead to substantial costs and infrastructure hurdles for countries with limited endoscopic infrastructure or gastroenterologists. Furthermore, our analysis suggests an immediate surge in GC diagnoses following a screening program, which will significantly burden treatment services. This necessitates a prompt healthcare system response, likely increasing demand for endoscopic submucosal dissection, which requires investment in training and infrastructure [ 31 ]. Finally, programs must address potential inequities in access to screening, diagnosis, and treatment to ensure effectiveness and avoid worsening health disparities [ 32 ].
Conclusion: This study found a higher GC incidence in Seoul, South Korea, after the organized GC screening program compared to the synthetic control. The magnitude of the difference expanded and peaked in the tenth year after the program’s start, then began to narrow. The alternative APC analysis indicated that the increase might finally reverse into a reduction effect. Healthcare sectors should anticipate an immediate increase in care demands following GC screening implementation. Future studies that comprehensively evaluate GC screening, reporting both mortality and incidence outcomes, are needed to assess the overall effectiveness and to investigate the potential for overdiagnosis, which remains an understudied possibility in GC screening.
